summary: The sole illustrative case (Access Cardiosystems) is a patent/invention-ownership dispute, not a work-for-hire (copyright) case, and patent law has no 'work made for hire' doctrine at all, so it only loosely illustrates the copyright-specific gap the clause is discussing.
evidence: Fetched opinion text: 'Inventorship and ownership present different legal questions and are governed by distinct areas of law... what is at issue in this case is the equitable ownership of the intellectual property, because it is undisputed that the legal ownership technically rests in Fincke as the named inventor.' The clause's own quote likewise calls Fincke 'the de facto owner of the invention disclosed in the '645 Application.' Patent ownership vests in the inventor regardless of employment or incorporation status absent an assignment; there is no employer work-for-hire default for patents the way 17 U.S.C. §101/201(b) provides for copyrightable works, so the case does not actually turn on (and does not illustrate) the work-for-hire 'employer' concept the clause above and this clause's own reasoning is built on.
suggestedFix: Either drop this case as an illustration of the work-for-hire pre-incorporation gap, or add a sentence clarifying that it illustrates a doctrinally distinct point (default personal ownership of inventions/patents absent assignment, which applies whether or not the company existed yet) rather than a copyright work-for-hire scenario.

summary: The body's comparison to a nonprofit public benefit corporation's dissolution procedure (superior-court decree with the Attorney General as a party) and to a federal tax 'organizational test' regulation is not supported by either citation in citations[]; both citations (§ 8713(a) and § 8717(a)-(b)) are purely mutual-benefit-corporation provisions and say nothing about public benefit corporations or federal tax law.
evidence: Clause body: "A nonprofit public benefit corporation's remaining assets, by contrast, are disposed of in conformity with its own articles or bylaws too, but subject to any charitable trust under which the assets are held and ordinarily only by a superior court decree in a proceeding to which the California Attorney General is a party -- and a related federal tax regulation treats an organization's assets as failing the federal tax-exemption \"organizational test\" if dissolution assets could go to the organization's own members." No citation in citations[] covers either half of this sentence; the gap paragraph discusses only §§ 8713/8717 and never mentions Cal. Corp. Code § 6716 or the federal regulation by name. (The underlying claim checks out: Cal. Corp. Code § 6716(b) provides "the disposition required in subdivision (a) shall be made by decree of the superior court of the proper county in proceedings to which the Attorney General is a party" (subject to a § 6716(c) AG-waiver exception), and 26 C.F.R. § 1.501(c)(3)-1(b)(4) states an organization "does not meet the organizational test if its articles or the law of the State in which it was created provide that its assets would, upon dissolution, be distributed to its members or shareholders." So the comparison is accurate, but it rests on two sources this clause never cites or discloses as additional sources, unlike the rest of this document's consistent practice of flagging every source it relies on.)
suggestedFix: Add a third and fourth citations[] entry for Cal. Corp. Code § 6716(b)-(c) and for 26 C.F.R. § 1.501(c)(3)-1(b)(4), each with its own quote, or shorten the body sentence to the bare fact already covered by the two cited sections and move the public-benefit/federal-tax comparison into the gap text as an acknowledged, separately-sourced aside.

summary: The clause's body describes the trade-secret/IP, source-code, and antitheft carve-outs as the express limits on the documentation-and-parts mandate, but Public Resources Code § 42488.2 contains at least one more express carve-out -- subdivision (g), excusing a manufacturer from selling service parts it no longer provides or makes available to authorized repair providers -- plus a further 'equivalent-or-better free replacement product' exception, neither of which appears anywhere in this document's clause set, so a reader of this 'Disclosure Limits Information Sheet' is left believing the four described carve-outs are the complete set of statutory limits on the mandate.
evidence: Clause body: "...the trade secret, intellectual property, source code, and antitheft carve-outs described elsewhere in this document operate as express limits on this same underlying mandate -- they do not create a separate or freestanding disclosure duty of their own." Contrast the statute itself (per search-engine-surfaced quote of § 42488.2(g)): "Nothing in this section shall be construed to require a manufacturer to sell service parts if the service parts are no longer provided by the manufacturer or made available to an authorized repair provider." The California Bureau of Household Goods and Services' official June 15, 2024 Right to Repair Act Industry Advisory independently confirms both omitted limitations: "Manufacturers DO NOT have to sell service parts if they no longer provide the service parts or make them available to authorized repair providers," and "Manufacturers DO NOT have to comply with SB 244 if they provide, at no charge to the consumer, a replacement product that is equivalent or better and is readily available."
sourceChecked: https://bhgs.dca.ca.gov/forms_pubs/sb_244_industry_advisory_english.pdf (fetched directly); § 42488.2(g) text surfaced via search engine snippet of codes.findlaw.com/law.justia.com (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov itself unreachable, Cloudflare 403 on both curl and WebFetch, and the section postdates the law.onecle.com mirror's 2017/2018 snapshot)
suggestedFix: Add a sibling clause (or expand this clause's gap text) disclosing § 42488.2(g)'s 'no-longer-provided service parts' carve-out and the separate free-equivalent-replacement-product exception, and revise this clause's body so it no longer reads as if the trade secret/IP, source code, and antitheft carve-outs are the only express limits on the mandate -- e.g., 'among other express carve-outs described in § 42488.2, not all of which are addressed in this document.'

summary: The clause offers 'the departing member was the sole member' as an example of a dissociation that coincides with a statutory dissolution trigger (the 90-consecutive-days-with-no-members rule), but the same statutory subsection it cites carves out exactly that scenario when the sole member dies, letting the membership interest pass automatically to heirs who become substituted members without triggering the no-members clock.
evidence: Live text of Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.01(c): "The passage of 90 consecutive days during which the limited liability company has no members, except that, on the death of a natural person who is the sole member of a limited liability company, the status of the member, including a membership interest, may pass to one or more heirs, successors, and assigns of the member by will or applicable law. An heir, successor, or assign of the member's interest becomes a substituted member pursuant to paragraph (4) of subdivision (c) of Section 17704.01 ... without the permission or consent of the heirs, successors, or assigns or those administering the estate of the deceased member." The clause's body nonetheless treats 'the departing member was the sole member' as an undifferentiated example of when dissociation (which it defines to include death) triggers dissolution.
suggestedFix: Replace the parenthetical with one that doesn't implicate the death carve-out (e.g., "for example, the departing member withdrew or was expelled while being the sole member"), or add a sentence noting that death of a sole member is treated differently: the statute lets the membership interest pass automatically to heirs who become substituted members, so that particular scenario does not necessarily start the 90-day no-members clock at all.

summary: The clause's gap note misdescribes the formula that CCP 706.050 used immediately before the September 1, 2023 amendment, claiming it was tied to 'federal poverty guidelines' when the actual predecessor formula was itself a minimum-wage multiple (25% of disposable earnings or 50% of the amount over 40 times the state minimum wage), not a poverty-guideline figure.
evidence: Clause's gap text: "which repealed and replaced a prior version of this section that had tied the exempt amount to federal poverty guidelines rather than to a multiple of the minimum wage." Contradicted by the actual prior statutory text (confirmed via an independent publisher's text of the predecessor version): "(a) Except as otherwise provided in this chapter, the maximum amount of disposable earnings of an individual judgment debtor for any workweek that is subject to levy under an earnings withholding order shall not exceed the lesser of the following: (1) Twenty-five percent of the individual’s disposable earnings for that week. (2) Fifty percent of the amount by which the individual’s disposable earnings for that week exceed 40 times the state minimum hourly wage in effect at the time the earnings are payable." A 2012 legislative analysis of AB 1775 likewise describes the baseline before that bill as conforming to the federal formula of '30 times the federal minimum wage' -- again a minimum-wage multiple, not a poverty-guideline figure, at every point in this provision's history that could be located. (A genuinely poverty-guideline-linked figure -- the CDSS 'minimum basic standard of adequate care for a family of four' -- does exist elsewhere in the Enforcement of Judgments Law, for the unrelated bank-account-levy exemption under a different section, which may be the source of the conflation.)
sourceChecked: https://law.onecle.com/california/civil-procedure/706.050.html; https://california.public.law/codes/code_of_civil_procedure_section_706.050 (confirms current 20%/48x text, 'updated Jan. 1, 2023'); web search of AB 1775 (2012) legislative analysis and SB 1477 (2022) history
suggestedFix: Replace the 'federal poverty guidelines' characterization with an accurate one, e.g.: "...which repealed and replaced a prior version of this section that capped withholding at the lesser of 25% of disposable earnings or 50% of the amount by which earnings exceeded 40 times the state minimum hourly wage -- a less protective minimum-wage-indexed formula, not a different kind of measure." Recheck against the official session-law text of Stats. 2022, Ch. 849 (SB 1477) and the immediately preceding version of § 706.050 before finalizing wording.

summary: The body paraphrases Welf. & Inst. Code § 15657.03(y) as excluding only civil-harassment (CCP § 527.6) and domestic-violence (Fam. Code Div. 10) proceedings, silently dropping the statute's third, equally express exclusion for Rosenthal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act proceedings (Civil Code Title 1.6C, commencing § 1788) — even though that exclusion is sitting in the clause's own quoted citation text.
evidence: Clause body: "Welfare and Institutions Code section 15657.03(y) states that section 15657.03 does not apply to any action or proceeding governed by Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 525) of Title 7 of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure — the chapter that includes California's civil harassment restraining order statute, Code of Civil Procedure section 527.6 — or by Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code, California's Domestic Violence Prevention Act." versus the clause's own cited statutory quote: "(y) This section does not apply to any action or proceeding governed by Title 1.6C (commencing with Section 1788) of Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code, Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 525) of Title 7 of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code." (Confirmed as the live, current text of § 15657.03(y) on 2026-10-31 via california.public.law's mirror of the statute, after leginfo.legislature.ca.gov itself returned a Cloudflare bot-challenge all session; Title 1.6C commencing § 1788 of the Civil Code is independently confirmed via web search to be the Rosenthal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, not a civil-harassment or domestic-violence statute.) Neither the body nor the gap discloses this third exclusion anywhere, so a reader who relies on the prose rather than re-parsing the citation block would come away thinking (y) names only two carve-outs.
suggestedFix: Add a sentence noting the statute's text also excludes proceedings under the Rosenthal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (Civil Code Title 1.6C, § 1788 et seq.), e.g.: "Section 15657.03(y) also excludes proceedings governed by the Rosenthal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (Civil Code Title 1.6C, commencing with Section 1788); this document does not address how that exclusion might apply to a given set of facts."
